title: Gibraltar
wiki_lead:
Gibraltar (  jih-BRAWL-tər, -⁠BROL-, Spanish: [xiβɾalˈtaɾ]) is a British Overseas Territory and city located near the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, on the Bay of Gibraltar, near the exit of the Mediterranean Sea into the Atlantic Ocean (Strait of Gibraltar). It has an area of 6.8 km2 (2.6 sq mi) and is bordered to the north by Spain (Campo de Gibraltar). The landscape is dominated by the Rock of Gibraltar, at the foot of which is a densely populated town area. Gibraltar is home to around 38,000 people, primarily Gibraltarians.
Gibraltar was founded as a permanent watchtower by the Almohads in 1160. It switched control between the Nasrids, Castilians and Marinids in the Late Middle Ages, acquiring larger strategic clout upon the destruction of nearby Algeciras c. 1375. It became again part of the Crown of Castile in 1462. In 1704, Anglo-Dutch forces captured Gibraltar from Spain during the War of the Spanish Succession, and it was ceded to Great Britain in perpetuity under the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713. It became an important base for the Royal Navy, particularly during the Napoleonic Wars and World War II, as it controlled the narrow entrance and exit to the Mediterranean Sea, the Strait of Gibraltar, with half the world's seaborne trade passing through it.
The sovereignty of Gibraltar is a point of contention in Anglo-Spanish relations as Spain asserts a claim to the territory. Gibraltarians overwhelmingly rejected proposals for Spanish sovereignty in a 1967 referendum, and for shared sovereignty in a 2002 referendum. Nevertheless, Gibraltar maintains close economic and cultural links with Spain, with many Gibraltarians speaking Spanish as well as a local dialect known as Llanito.
Gibraltar's economy rests on online gambling, financial services, tourism and the port. With one of the world's lowest unemployment rates, the largest part of the labour force are resident in Spain or non-Gibraltarians, especially in the private sector.
Since Brexit, Gibraltar is not a member of the European Union: a draft treaty was negotiated in June 2025 that would allow the territory to participate in the Schengen Agreement and the European Union customs union. In July 2026, the UK, Spain, Gibraltar and the EU signed the treaty, removing border controls with Spain.

Name
The name is derived from Arabic: جبل طارق, romanized: Jabal Ṭāriq, lit. 'Mount of Tariq' (named after the 8th-century North African military leader Tariq ibn Ziyad, who began the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula via the Strait of Gibraltar in 711).


History


Prehistory and ancient history
Evidence of Neanderthal habitation in Gibraltar from around 50,000 years ago has been discovered at Gorham's Cave. The caves of Gibraltar continued to be used by Homo sapiens after the final extinction of the Neanderthals. Stone tools, ancient hearths and animal bones dating from around 40,000 years ago to about 5,000 years ago have been found in deposits left in Gorham's Cave.
Numerous potsherds dating from the Neolithic period have been found in Gibraltar's caves, mostly of types typical of the Almerian culture found elsewhere in Andalusia, especially around the town of Almería, from which it takes its name. There is little evidence of habitation in the Bronze Age when people had largely stopped living in caves.
During ancient times, Gibraltar was regarded by the peoples of the Mediterranean as a place of religious and symbolic importance. The Phoenicians were present for several centuries since around 950 BC, apparently using Gorham's Cave as a shrine to the genius loci, as did the Carthaginians and Romans after them. Gibraltar was known as Mons Calpe, a name perhaps of Phoenician origin. Mons Calpe was considered by the ancient Greeks and Romans as one of the Pillars of Hercules, after the Greek legend of the creation of the Strait of Gibraltar by Heracles. grok_lead: Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory comprising a fortified peninsula of 6.5 square kilometers at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, strategically positioned at the western entrance to the Mediterranean Sea where it meets the Atlantic Ocean through the Strait of Gibraltar. The territory is dominated by the Rock of Gibraltar, a 426-meter limestone ridge that has served as a natural fortress and military stronghold throughout history. Its population stands at approximately 32,000 registered Gibraltarians, supported by a working population including daily commuters from Spain, in one of the world's most densely populated areas. Gibraltar was captured from Spain by Anglo-Dutch forces in 1704 during the War of the Spanish Succession and formally ceded to Britain in perpetuity under Article X of the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713, with stipulations limiting territorial expansion and granting Spain a right of first refusal should Britain relinquish control. The territory operates under a Westminster-style parliamentary system with internal self-government, while the United Kingdom retains responsibility for defense, external affairs, and internal security; its head of state is the British monarch, represented by a governor. Gibraltar's economy, with a GDP of Â£2.347 billion, relies on pillars including financial services, online gaming, maritime operations, and tourism, bolstered by a low-tax regime that attracts international business without dependence on UK aid. Sovereignty remains a point of contention with Spain, which asserts historical claims despite the Utrecht cession, leading to periodic border restrictions and diplomatic friction; however, Gibraltarians have consistently affirmed their preference for British status, rejecting Spanish sovereignty by 99.2% in a 1967 referendum and shared UK-Spanish sovereignty by 98.9% in 2002. The territory's multicultural society, reflecting British, Spanish, Genoese, Maltese, and other influences, speaks English officially alongside the creole Llanito and maintains a diverse religious landscape including Catholic, Anglican, Jewish, Hindu, and Muslim communities. Gibraltar's strategic port and airfield have historically underpinned its military significance, including roles in World War II operations, while its unique ecology features Barbary macaques and endemic flora adapted to the Rock's karst terrain.
